claims.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys can combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Computational optimization using CALPHAD, molecular dynamics, and density functional theory can help optimize lightweight-HEA composition and microstructure.
Incorporating carbon nanotubes or graphene can help lightweight HEAs achieve the proposed combination of properties.
Grain size, phase distribution, and interface properties mediate the effects of composition optimization and nanomaterial reinforcement.
Solid-solution strengthening contributes to improved mechanical properties.
Grain-boundary strengthening contributes to improved mechanical properties.
Effective load transfer across nanomaterial–HEA interfaces contributes to improved mechanical properties.
The optimized and nanomaterial-reinforced alloys will have greater mechanical strength than the baseline alloys.
The optimized and nanomaterial-reinforced alloys will have greater corrosion resistance than the baseline alloys.
The optimized and nanomaterial-reinforced alloys will have greater high-temperature oxidation resistance than the baseline alloys.
The proposed property improvements are expected under high-temperature exposure, corrosive environments, and mechanical loading.
CALPHAD has accuracy and applicability limitations for lightweight-HEA design, including missing lightweight elements and inability to directly predict important mechanical properties.
Molecular-dynamics predictions for lightweight HEAs are limited by uncertain interatomic potentials and accessible time and length scales.
Excessive carbon-nanotube content can cause agglomeration and degrade mechanical properties.
Nanomaterial–alloy interface quality limits the effectiveness of load transfer.
Failure to obtain significant improvements in all three measured properties relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
